about: The city of Rome as the Rome world's hub (places_rome.gd): the whole city, walked on the map of content/rome/republican_rome.json (real metres east and north of the Forum, shrunk by its scale). It stands in one of four ages; a monument stands from the year it was built ('from'), is a ruin from 'ruin', and is gone from 'gone'. Years are negative before Christ. Positions not marked in republican_rome.json are read off modern coordinates of the remains and are approximate. 'walkable' is the part of the city you can walk in (the Servian city, the Forum Boarium and the southern Campus Martius); beyond it, up to 'outer' (the line of Aurelian's wall), the city goes on to be seen, not walked.

ages.name: The Republic
ages.line: Rome, 201 BC. Hannibal is beaten at Zama; Carthage has given up its fleet. The legions come home. A city of tufa and temples, poor, proud, and certain of its gods.
ages.navel: Let the years pass: to the last generation of the Republic

ages.name: The Late Republic
ages.line: Rome, about 50 BC. The Republic rules the world and can no longer rule itself. Gangs in the streets, votes for sale, armies loyal to their generals. Pompey's theatre is new; Caesar is in Gaul.
ages.navel: Let the years pass: to the Empire at its height

ages.name: The Empire
ages.line: Rome, about AD 150, under Antoninus Pius: a city of perhaps a million, marble over brick, two years past its nine hundredth birthday.
ages.navel: Let the years pass: to the late Empire

ages.name: The Late Empire
ages.line: Rome, about AD 330: Constantine has built a new Rome on the Bosporus. The old one keeps its Senate, its games and its walls, and now its churches.
ages.navel: Let the years pass: to the emptied city

ages.name: The Fall
ages.line: Rome, AD 552, at the end of the Gothic War: besieged, taken and emptied again and again. The aqueducts are cut. A few thousand live by the river.

navel.name: The Navel of the City (Umbilicus Urbis)
navel.note: The round stone that marks the centre of Rome, beside the Rostra. Every road, it was said, began here.

abitato.note: In the 6th century the people drew in to the bend of the Tiber in the Campus Martius, near the river and its mills, when the aqueducts failed.

aurelian_wall.note: Aurelian's wall, begun AD 271 against the barbarians: 19 km of brick, raised higher under Honorius.

open.why: the open Campus Martius, where the army mustered and the people voted

roads.name: the Argiletum and the Clivus Suburanus

bridges.name: the Sublician Bridge
bridges.note: The oldest bridge, all of wood and not an iron nail in it, as religion required: the one Horatius held.

bridges.name: the Aemilian Bridge
bridges.note: The first stone bridge over the Tiber, 142 BC.

bridges.name: the Fabrician Bridge
bridges.note: Lucius Fabricius, keeper of the roads, built it to the island in 62 BC. It still carries people today.

bridges.name: the Cestian Bridge
bridges.note: From the island to the far bank.

regions.empire: Regio IV, the Temple of Peace and the Subura

regions.republic: Collina, the Quirinal and the Viminal
The Via Lata, outside the wall

monuments.name: the Temple of Jupiter Best and Greatest
monuments.note: The greatest temple of Rome, on the Capitol: Jupiter in the middle, Juno and Minerva either side. Triumphs end here.
monuments.fall: The Vandals stripped its gilded bronze roof tiles in 455. The temple of the city's god stands open to the sky.

monuments.name: the Temple of Juno Moneta
monuments.note: Juno the Warner, on the Citadel. The mint stands beside her, and so the word money.

monuments.name: the Tabularium
monuments.note: The record office, 78 BC: the state's laws and treaties on bronze, behind a great arcade over the Forum.

monuments.name: the Temple of Saturn
monuments.note: The oldest temple in the Forum. Under its podium is the treasury of the Roman people.
monuments.fall: Rebuilt after a fire in the 4th century with columns taken from other buildings. Now only its porch stands.

monuments.name: the Temple of Concord
monuments.note: Built in 121 BC after the killing of Gaius Gracchus, to celebrate a concord the murder had made.

monuments.name: the Temple of Vespasian and Titus
the Temple of Castor and Pollux
monuments.note: The twin horsemen who watered their horses at the spring of Juturna here, bringing news of victory at Lake Regillus.

monuments.name: the Temple of Vesta
monuments.note: The round house of the hearth of Rome. Six Vestal Virgins keep its fire burning; if it goes out, Rome is in danger.
monuments.fall: Theodosius closed the temple and the fire went out in 394.

monuments.name: the Regia
monuments.note: The house of the kings, then of the chief priest, the Pontifex Maximus. Caesar holds the office.

monuments.name: the Rostra
monuments.note: The speakers' platform, faced with the bronze beaks of ships taken at Antium in 338 BC.

monuments.name: the Senate House
monuments.note: The Senate House. Clodius' supporters burned it with his body in 52 BC; Faustus Sulla is building it again.

monuments.name: the Senate House (Curia Julia)
monuments.note: Caesar's Senate House, finished by Augustus. Inside, the altar and statue of Victory.
monuments.fall: The Senate still meets, a few old families; in a few years it will be gone from the sources.

monuments.name: the Basilica Aemilia
monuments.note: A great hall for the law and for business, with the money-changers' shops along its front.
monuments.fall: Burned when Alaric's Goths sacked Rome in 410. Coins melted into its floor are still there.

monuments.name: the Basilica Julia
monuments.note: Caesar's basilica. The Centumviral court hears inheritance cases here; idlers scratch game boards into its steps.

monuments.name: the Temple of the Deified Julius
monuments.note: Built where Caesar's body was burned by the crowd in 44 BC. The first Roman to be made a god.

monuments.name: the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina
monuments.note: Antoninus built it for his wife Faustina, dead in 141. When he dies the Senate will add his name.
monuments.fall: Its porch stands whole. In a few centuries it will be a church, and it still is.

monuments.name: the Shrine of Janus
monuments.note: The twin doors of Janus stand open while Rome is at war, and close only in peace. They are almost never closed.

monuments.name: the Arch of Septimius Severus
monuments.note: Severus' arch, 203, for his wars in Parthia. The name of his son Geta was chiselled out after Caracalla killed him.

monuments.name: the Arch of Titus
monuments.note: For the taking of Jerusalem in 70. Inside, the relief of the Temple's menorah carried in triumph.

monuments.name: the Arch of Constantine
monuments.note: Constantine's arch, 315, for his victory over Maxentius at the Milvian Bridge. Much of its sculpture is taken from older monuments.

monuments.name: the Temple of Venus and Rome
monuments.note: Hadrian's own design: Venus, mother of Rome, and Roma, back to back. The largest temple in the city. ROMA backwards is AMOR.

monuments.name: the Basilica of Maxentius
monuments.note: Begun by Maxentius, finished by Constantine: vaults so wide they taught the builders of St Peter's.

monuments.name: the Temple of Peace
monuments.note: Vespasian's garden square of peace, with the spoils of Jerusalem and a library. The marble plan of Rome hangs on one wall.
monuments.fall: Part of its library hall has been a church of Saints Cosmas and Damian since 527.

monuments.name: the Forum of Caesar
monuments.note: Caesar's square, paid for with Gallic gold.

monuments.name: the Temple of Venus the Mother
monuments.note: Venus Genetrix, from whom Caesar's family claims descent through Aeneas. He vowed her this temple at Pharsalus.

monuments.name: the Forum of Augustus
monuments.note: Augustus' square, with statues of the great men of Rome down its colonnades.

monuments.name: the Temple of Mars the Avenger
monuments.note: Vowed by the young Octavian at Philippi, to avenge Caesar. Generals set out for war from here.
monuments.fall: Its roof is gone; its high fire wall still shuts out the Subura behind it.

monuments.name: the Forum of Trajan
monuments.note: The last and grandest of the imperial fora, paid for with the gold of Dacia. Ammianus says Constantius II stood speechless in it.

monuments.name: Trajan's Column
monuments.note: A hundred Roman feet high, its spiral frieze tells the Dacian wars in 2,500 figures. Trajan's ashes lie in its base.

monuments.name: Trajan's Markets
monuments.note: A hemicycle of brick shops cut into the Quirinal: pepper, oil, wine, the grain office.

monuments.name: the Flavian Amphitheatre
monuments.note: The Flavian Amphitheatre: fifty thousand watch the games. Titus opened it in 80 with a hundred days of them.
monuments.fall: Earthquakes cracked it in 443 and 484. The last beast hunt was in 523. People are moving into its arches.

monuments.name: the Colossus
monuments.note: Nero's bronze statue of himself, 30 m high, made the Sun by Vespasian. The amphitheatre is named for it: the Colosseum.

monuments.name: the Meta Sudans
monuments.note: The Sweating Post: a tall cone fountain, like a turning post of the circus, running with water.

monuments.name: the Baths of Trajan
monuments.note: Built over Nero's Golden House, buried to make them. The first of the great imperial baths.

monuments.name: the Baths of Caracalla
monuments.note: 1,600 bathers at once: hot rooms, cold pool, gymnasia, libraries, gardens.
monuments.fall: The Goths cut the aqueducts in 537. With no water the baths are empty halls.

monuments.name: the Baths of Diocletian
monuments.note: The largest baths of all, for 3,000. Tradition says Christian prisoners built them.

monuments.name: the Palace of the Caesars
monuments.note: Domitian's palace, the Domus Augustana: the word palace comes from this hill, the Palatium.

monuments.name: the houses of the great on the Palatine
monuments.note: The hill of the rich: Cicero, Crassus, Clodius and Hortensius all have houses here.

monuments.name: the Temple of the Great Mother
monuments.note: Cybele, brought from Phrygia in 204 BC as a black stone, to win the war against Hannibal.

monuments.name: the Temple of Apollo on the Palatine
monuments.note: Augustus' temple to Apollo, beside his own house, with Greek and Latin libraries.

monuments.name: the Circus Maximus
monuments.note: The great racecourse: 150,000 in the stands, later perhaps a quarter of a million. The Reds, Whites, Greens and Blues.
monuments.fall: The last recorded races were held in 549, under Totila the Goth.

monuments.name: the obelisk of the Circus
monuments.note: Brought from Heliopolis by Augustus after the conquest of Egypt, set on the spina of the Circus.

monuments.name: the Temple of Ceres, Liber and Libera
monuments.note: The plebs' own temple, and the office of their aediles. The grain goddess.

monuments.name: the Temple of Diana on the Aventine
the Temple of Juno the Queen
monuments.note: Juno of Veii, invited to Rome when the city fell in 396 BC. The statue, they say, nodded.

monuments.name: the Temple of Hercules the Victor
monuments.note: The round marble temple of the cattle market, the oldest marble building in Rome. It still stands.

monuments.name: the Temple of Portunus
monuments.note: The god of harbours, by the river port. It still stands, because it became a church.

monuments.name: the Temples of Fortune and Mother Dawn
the Temple of Aesculapius
monuments.note: The god of healing came from Epidaurus as a snake in 291 BC and chose the island. The sick still sleep here.

monuments.name: the Theatre of Marcellus
monuments.note: Augustus' theatre, named for his nephew Marcellus, dead young. 20,000 seats.
monuments.fall: A fortress in waiting: in centuries to come families will live in its arches, and still do.

monuments.name: the Temple of Bellona
monuments.note: The Senate meets here, outside the sacred boundary, to receive generals who may not yet enter the city.

monuments.name: the Temple of Apollo the Healer
the Flaminian Circus
monuments.note: An open field for the Plebeian Games and for triumphs gathering before they march.

monuments.name: the Temple of Mars in the Circus
monuments.note: Mars of the army, beside the Flaminian Circus, where the army mustered outside the city.

monuments.name: the Theatre of Pompey
monuments.note: The first stone theatre in Rome, 55 BC. To get round the ban on permanent theatres, Pompey set a temple of Venus on top of the seats.

monuments.name: the Temple of Venus the Victor
monuments.note: Venus Victrix, on top of Pompey's theatre: the seats are the stair to her temple.

monuments.name: the Portico of Pompey
monuments.note: Behind the theatre: a garden portico, and at its far end the hall where the Senate met on the Ides of March, 44 BC.

monuments.name: the Voting Pens (Saepta)
monuments.note: The great enclosure where the people once voted by tribes. Under the emperors, a market of luxury goods.

monuments.name: the Villa Publica
monuments.note: Where the censors count the citizens and generals wait for their triumph.

monuments.name: the Pantheon
monuments.note: Hadrian's temple of all the gods: a dome 43 m across with an open eye at the top. No one has built a larger dome of concrete since.
monuments.fall: Shut, and falling to no one. In 609 the Pope will make it a church, and that will save it.

monuments.name: the Temple of Isis
monuments.note: Isis and Serapis of Egypt, with obelisks and sphinxes. Her priests shave their heads; her rites are open to women and slaves.

monuments.name: the Stadium of Domitian
monuments.note: A Greek stadium for athletics, 30,000 seats. Its oval is still the shape of the Piazza Navona.

monuments.name: the Temple of the Deified Hadrian
the Temple of the Sun
monuments.note: Aurelian's temple of the Unconquered Sun, built with the treasure of Palmyra. His feast is 25 December.

monuments.name: the Altar of Augustan Peace
monuments.note: The Senate's altar to the peace Augustus brought, 9 BC: the imperial family in procession in marble.

monuments.name: the Mausoleum of Augustus
monuments.note: The round tomb of Augustus and his family, 90 m across, his bronze statue on top. His deeds are cut on bronze at the door.
monuments.fall: Alaric's Goths looted it in 410 and scattered the ashes.

monuments.name: the Mausoleum of Hadrian
monuments.note: Hadrian's tomb across the river, where the emperors lie until Caracalla.
monuments.fall: A fortress now. In 537 the Greek garrison broke its statues and threw them down on the Goths.

monuments.name: the Temple of Quirinus
monuments.note: Quirinus, who was Romulus made a god, on the hill that bears his name.

monuments.name: the Temple of the Deified Claudius
the Temple of Jupiter the Stayer
monuments.note: Romulus vowed it when the Romans ran from the Sabines, if Jupiter would stay their flight. Cicero spoke against Catiline in it.

monuments.name: the Lateran Basilica
monuments.note: Constantine's gift to the bishop of Rome, on the site of his horse guards' barracks: the cathedral of the Pope.
monuments.fall: The Pope's own church and house. Grain for the poor is handed out from the church's farms.

monuments.name: the Basilica of St Peter
monuments.note: Constantine's great church over the grave of the apostle Peter, on the Vatican hill across the river.

monuments.name: the church of Holy Mary the Old
monuments.note: A hall at the foot of the Palatine made a church in the 6th century, its walls painted with saints.

monuments.name: the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian
the church of the Holy Cross
monuments.note: The empress Helena's palace hall, holding the pieces of the Cross she brought from Jerusalem.

republic: Patrician: Pompey is master of Rome, and Caesar has an army of veterans in Gaul.
Plebeian: Caesar gave us land and the free games. What did Pompey give us?
Patrician: Order, which you do not know how to value.
Shopkeeper: The interest on my loan is twelve a hundred a year.
Neighbour: Catiline promised to cancel all debts. Look how he ended.
Client: My patron will speak for me in court. He learned his art from the Greeks.
Friend: And from the Rhetorica. Invention, arrangement, style, memory, delivery.
Freedman: My master freed me in his will. Now I'm a citizen, and my son may be a knight.
Slave: And I carry your baskets.
Old man: When I was young no senator would be seen at the games.
Young man: Now they pay for them. How else do you get elected?
empire: Patrician: The emperor asks the Senate's advice. It is a courtesy, and we are grateful.
Plebeian: You're grateful. We just want the grain ships on time.
Greek: Your poet Juvenal says Rome is a Greek city now.
Roman: Juvenal complains about everything. Pass the oil.
Baker: Another fire in the Subura last night.
Watchman: Top floor, as always. A lamp, a straw mattress, six floors of timber.
Gladiator fan: Did you see the net-fighter yesterday?
Friend: The crowd spared him. He fought well.
Mother: My son will be a lawyer and argue in the Basilica Julia.
Neighbour: Then teach him to speak, and to remember his speech.
late: Senator: They say the gods left Rome when Constantine turned his back on them.
Christian: God is not a Roman. He is everywhere, even here.
Blue: The Emperor is in the East and the Prefect fears the crowd more than the barbarians.
Green: As he should. We are Rome.
Old man: My grandfather saw Aurelian's triumph, with Queen Zenobia of Palmyra walking in gold chains.
Boy: Is it true the chains were so heavy she had to be helped?
fall: Monk: The Pope asks us to give bread.
Woman: There is so little, Father, and so many hungry.
Soldier: Narses beat Totila at Busta Gallorum. The Goth is dead.
Old man: And Rome? Who will give us back Rome?
Old woman: A bath, they say. Hot water for everyone. I never saw it.
